I'm a vegetarian, but I didn't do it for the ethical reasons (although I don't think I could eat meat again because of my ethics), and I didn't do it for health reasons. I did it because it was a Wednesday.

I simply decided one day, with no previous thoughts about it, to throw away all meat from my refrigerator and be a vegetarian. It's now been over 6 months, and while I've slipped up a few times, I'm still going strong.

So I want to know if anyone else has become a vegetarian/vegan just because like me, and if there are even stranger reasons behind it.
Why did you become a vegetarian/vegan?

One day, I was just thinking (don't remember how the thought was triggered) and I just couldn't figure out how can person continue killing/eating animals when there's alternative out there which is even healthier than eating meat. I just couldn't give myself a reason to continue with the murder. For a few moments I was really confused. I really love animals, but at the same time I'm eating them, and somehow the society we live in made that feels ok. Obviously, I refused to continue eating meat only for the taste, and later figured out that the taste is also driven by what we're used to, and what we are thought (it's a cultural thing).

My family was worried about me, but I kept doing my own research all over the internet and kept meeting people that are vegetarian/vegan for a long period. All the facts are leading that the vegan is the way to go. For more than 10 years now I'm vegetarian, being (almost) vegan for the last few months. I'm now sure that vegan is the way to go, but vegetarianism is a good stepping stone.

Killing someone, so you can eat him, is totally absurd for my level of thinking. If we want to advance as species, we have to abandon that. This is the reason #1 for me and it will always be. Other reasons are healthy nutrition, ecology, etc.

Abusing animals is also really bad. Just visit some local farm and try to think with a clear mind. Animal farms are no different than matrix for the animals. That thing is so wrong it is insane. I can understand that at some point survival made people do very wicked things, but during the process of civilization, now is the time to move on for many reasons..
The thought of eating something that used to be alive makes me feel queasy.

I was in Disney eating one of those turkey legs. Just the feeling of its ligaments ripping made me so grossed out. I just haven't been able to look at meat the same way... the tendons and ligaments just cringes me out so much

Well, I was born a vegetarian. I'm from a Hindu family of the Brahmin sect which has predominantly been vegetarian throughout history (or at least so my family tells me).

So initially it was just that I knew little else. It was just what I knew. Then, when I was older and in school, I had the option to eat meat when I had money and everyone around me eating meat. My sister does, for example. But I decided not to on the grounds that it would hurt my parents, and why ruin a good thing you have going anyway? Lots of people struggle so hard to be vegetarian. It's healthy.

Eventually, as I've grown older, I've become ethically opposed to eating meat. Why? Firstly, it causes suffering. Secondly, it's ecologically prudent, and thirdly, I don't know where the animals go when they die. Yes, there is no evidence for an afterlife, but absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. I like to cover as many bases as possible. If I'm condemning them to an afterlife of misery, I'd feel very bad about myself.

Currently, I'm trying my best to go vegan. I've completely eliminated eggs out of my diet (my family is slightly unorthodox in that we eat eggs), and I'm trying to phase dairy out too, although it's proving to be much, much harder due to it's nutritional importance and convenience to me as a vegetarian.

I was raised in a home where meat was served at every meal of the day. I never considered the effect it had on anything because it was very normalized in my family.

Then I took an environmental science class as a freshman in college and the professor made a convincing argument for reducing the amount of meat you eat in order to have a positive impact on the environment. The argument he made at the time (which obviously can be improved), was that you can basically get all the protein you need from a couple of cans of tuna fish a week. Somehow that got me thinking about how it might not be so hard to cut back a bit. Eventually, I gave up red meat, then then chicken, and then soon after I was a full vegetarian. It was a long slow process over a couple years. It was only later that I started to think about the amount of suffering caused by the meat-producing system, and that only reinforced my beliefs. That was 20 years ago.

Learning that it takes 5 times the amount of energy to produce a pound of meat to a pound of vegetables made me realize we could feed everyone with vegetables. Also, I wouldn't personally raise a pig or cow and be able to slaughter them so I shouldn't be promoting someone else to do it for me.

I know this is going to sound like the stereotypical "I was in a college class reason", but I was in a Environmental Ethics class, and I realized the sad impact the meat industry had on the environment then shortly there after learned of the horrors of CAFOS, and decided that eating meat didn't actually allign with the morals I had held the majority of my life.
